Abstract

Objective: Create a diagnostic algorithm in the HRS 2016 HCAP sample, and apply the algorithm to the HRS 2016-2022 waves.

Blom transformation

This script derives a normed, Blom-transformed version of the cognitive factor score (PF) for the 2016 HRS HCAP data, using restricted cubic splines to flexibly model the relationship between the raw factor score and its normalized (Blom) rank, and then applies that model to the full 2016 sample and the 2016–2022 longitudinal sample.

Inputs

Object Source file Description
hrs16_merged A7_050_hrs16_merged.rds Full 2016 HCAP merged dataset
hrs16_22_long A7_050_hrs16_22_long.rds Long-format 2016–2022 panel data

Step 1: Define the Normative Sample

  • Restricts to respondents not excluded from norming (normexcld == 0).
  • Creates a zero-filled version of the HCAP 2016 weight (HCAP16WGTR0), replacing NA weights with 0.

Step 2: Build Restricted Cubic Spline Terms

A helper function, factor_splines(df, q), computes a 3-term restricted cubic spline basis for the factor score PF, given four knot locations q:

  • spF1 — linear term (equal to PF itself)
  • spF2, spF3 — nonlinear spline basis terms, computed with the standard restricted cubic spline (natural spline) formula using knots k1–k4
  • Variable labels are attached to the three spline columns for documentation

Knots are set at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles of PF in the normative sample:

The spline basis is then generated for all three data frames, using the same knots derived from the norming sample:

  • hrs16_cog_norm — the normative sample
  • hrs16_merged — the full 2016 HCAP sample
  • hrs16_22_long — the 2016–2022 long panel (temporarily renaming F to PF to reuse the function, then dropping PF afterward)

Step 3: Blom Transform in the Normative Sample

  • Computes the Blom-transformed (normal-scores) version of PF within the normative sample only, using rcompanion::blom().

Step 4: Fit and Apply the Norming Model

A linear model predicts the Blom-transformed score from the spline basis:

F → Pblom

This model — fit only on the normative sample — is then used to generate predicted (“normed”) Blom scores (Pblom) for all three data frames.

  • hrs16_cog_norm$Pblom
  • hrs16_merged$Pblom
  • hrs16_22_long$Pblom

Each Pblom column is labelled: “Predicted Blom score (model from HCAP normal sample)”.

This approach effectively norms the factor score against the HCAP normative sample, allowing scores from the broader 2016 sample and the 2016–2022 panel to be expressed on the same normalized scale.

Outputs

Object Saved to
hrs16_cog_norm A7_052_hrs16_cog_norm.rds
hrs16_merged A7_052_hrs16_merged.rds
hrs16_22_long A7_052_hrs16_22_long.rds

Key Methodological Notes

  • Knots and model are derived solely from the normative sample (normexcld == 0), then applied out-of-sample to the full 2016 data and the longitudinal panel — this is the core “norming” step.
  • The restricted cubic spline uses a 3-degree-of-freedom formulation (1 linear + 2 nonlinear terms) based on 4 knots, a standard approach (e.g., Harrell’s rcs) for flexibly modeling non-linear relationships while keeping tails linear.
  • The Blom transformation converts the factor score to approximate normal scores (ranks transformed via the inverse normal CDF with the Blom correction), which is then predicted from the spline terms so it can be applied to samples outside the normative group.

Converting 2016-2022 waves to ‘long’ data format

This script takes several groups of wave-wide variables from the merged 2016–2022 dataset, pivots each group to long format (one row per person-wave), and merges them onto the existing long-format panel hrs16_22_long.

The four HRS/HCAP wave letters used throughout are:

  • P = 2016
  • Q = 2018
  • R = 2020
  • S = 2022

Inputs

Object Source file Description
hrs16_22_long A7_052_hrs16_22_long.rds Existing long-format 2016–2022 panel (one row per id-wave)
hrs16_22_merged A7_005_hrs16_22_merged.rds Wide-format merged dataset (one row per id, wave-prefixed columns)

Step 1: Pivot Simple “x” Variables

  • Selects columns matching the pattern x + wave letter + single digit (e.g. xP1, xQ2, …).
  • These are the demographic variables.
  • Uses pivot_longer() with .value to split each column name into a wave (P/Q/R/S) and a variable number (1, 2, …), creating one row per id-wave.
  • Since .value pivoting drops the x prefix from the resulting column names, rename_with() re-adds the x prefix (e.g. resulting columns become x1, x2, …).

Step 2: Pivot Interaction Variables

  • Selects interaction-term columns with a double wave/number pattern (e.g. xP1xP4).
  • These are the interaction between demographic variables.
  • Renames each column from the raw format (xP1xP4) to a standardized format (P_x1x4), moving the wave letter to the front so it can be extracted during pivoting.
  • Pivots to long format using .value, splitting each column into wave and the remaining interaction variable name (e.g. x1x4), producing one row per id-wave.

Step 3: Merge Simple and Interaction Variables

Combines the reshaped simple x variables and interaction variables into a single long data frame keyed by id and wave.

Step 4: Pivot the Jorm Cognitive Score

Reshapes the four wave-specific Jorm score columns (rPjorm, rQjorm, rRjorm, rSjorm) into a single jorm column with a wave identifier.

Step 5: Pivot the D102 (Imputed) Variable

Reshapes the four wave-specific imputed D102 columns into a single D102_imp column with a wave identifier.

Step 6: Merge Everything into the Long Panel

Sequentially left-joins the three newly reshaped long data frames onto the existing hrs16_22_long panel, keyed by id and wave, adding the x* variables, interaction terms, jorm score, and D102_imp as new columns.

Output

Object Saved to
hrs16_22_long A7_053_hrs16_22_long.rds

Key Methodological Notes

  • The core technique throughout is wide-to-long reshaping with tidyr::pivot_longer() using the .value sentinel, which lets a single call split column names into both an identifier (wave) and a variable name, avoiding manual loops over waves.
  • Regex patterns (names_pattern / matches()) are used consistently to select and parse wave-prefixed or wave-embedded column names for the four HRS waves (P/Q/R/S).
  • Column renaming (rename_with(), str_replace_all()) is used before pivoting when the wave identifier isn’t in a position pivot_longer() can parse directly (as with the interaction terms, where the wave letter needs to move to the front of the name).
  • All reshaped pieces are joined back to the master long panel using the composite key id + wave, preserving one row per person per wave.

Norming Factor Scores

This script builds a survey-weighted regression model predicting the normed Blom factor score (Pblom) from demographic/interaction variables, using the 2016 HCAP normative sample. It then applies that model to generate demographically-adjusted expected scores (Eblom) across all three data frames, and converts the residual (observed minus expected, standardized) into a T-scaled score (TF, mean 50, SD 10) — a common approach for producing norm-referenced cognitive scores adjusted for demographic characteristics.

Inputs

Object Source file Description
hrs16_cog_norm A7_052_hrs16_cog_norm.rds Normative HCAP 2016 sample with Pblom
hrs16_merged A7_052_hrs16_merged.rds Full 2016 HCAP sample with Pblom
hrs16_22_long A7_053_hrs16_22_long.rds Long-format 2016–2022 panel

Step 1: Alias Wave-P (“2016”) Variables to Generic Names

  • Both hrs16_cog_norm and hrs16_merged are cross-sectional 2016 (wave P) data, so their wave-P-prefixed variables (xP1…xP7 and interaction terms like xP1xP4) are copied into generic, wave-agnostic names (x1…x7, x1x4, etc.).
  • This lets the same model formula be applied consistently to the 2016 cross-sectional data and the long panel (hrs16_22_long), which already stores these variables under the generic x* names (from the earlier reshape in A7_053).

Step 2: Fit the Demographic Model (Survey-Weighted)

  • Defines the complex survey design (SECU primary sampling unit, STRATUM strata, HCAP16WGTR0 weights) for the normative sample.
  • Fits a survey-weighted GLM predicting Pblom from the seven main-effect demographic terms (x1–x7) and a set of pairwise interaction terms — fit only on the normative sample, mirroring the norming approach used for Pblom itself.

Step 3: Predict Expected (“Eblom”) Scores in All Samples

  • Uses the fitted model to generate demographically-expected Blom scores (Eblom) for the normative sample and the full 2016 sample.

For the long panel, predictions are generated on a filtered subset (rows with non-missing x1, i.e. rows with demographic data available) and then merged back:

  • This avoids errors from augment()/predict() on rows with missing predictors, then reattaches Eblom by id + wave, leaving NA for waves without demographic data.

Step 4: Compute R² and Residual SD for Standardization

  • Computes a pseudo-R² for the survey GLM as 1 - deviance/null.deviance (~0.366).
  • Computes the weighted standard deviation of Pblom in the normative sample (~0.973) using Hmisc::wtd.var().
  • Combines these to get the standardized residual SD (~0.775), which is used as the scaling denominator in the T-score formula below.

Step 5: Compute T-Scaled Residual Score (TF)

Applied identically to all three data frames:

  • TF is a T-score (mean 50, SD 10) representing how far a person’s observed Blom score (Pblom) deviates from their demographically-expected score (Eblom), standardized by the residual SD.
  • This produces a cognitive score that is normed against the HCAP sample and adjusted for demographic characteristics (age, sex, race/ethnicity, education).

Outputs

Object Saved to
hrs16_merged A7_055_hrs16_merged.rds
hrs16_cog_norm A7_055_hrs16_cog_norm.rds
hrs16_22_long A7_055_hrs16_22_long.rds
foo_glm (fitted model) A7_055_foo_lm.rds

Key Methodological Notes

  • The model is fit only in the normative sample using survey weights and design, consistent with proper norming methodology, then applied out-of-sample to the full 2016 data and the 2016–2022 panel — the same “fit-in-norm, apply-to-all” pattern used for the Blom transform in the prior script (A7_052).
  • The wave-P variable aliasing step (Step 1) is necessary because the 2016 cross-sectional frames store demographic/interaction variables with a xP* prefix, while the long panel already uses generic x* names — aliasing lets one model formula work across all three data structures.
  • TF is analogous to a standardized residual T-score: values above 50 indicate better-than-expected cognitive performance given demographics, values below 50 indicate worse-than-expected performance, in SD-of-10 units.
  • Missing-data handling for the long panel (filtering to !is.na(x1) before prediction, then left-joining back) preserves all panel rows while avoiding prediction errors on waves lacking demographic covariates.

Apply algorithm in the HCAP sample

This section descrbes a rule-based classification algorithm applied to the HCAP subsample to assign each respondent to one of three cognitive status categories: Normal, MCI, or Dementia. The algorithm combines a T-scaled cognitive performance score (TF), a self-reported memory change item (PD102), and an informant-rated cognitive change score (jorm). A flow diagram counting function is also defined to document how many respondents pass through each decision node. Both algorithm_thresholds and v1_algorithm are saved as function objects, allowing identical classification logic to be applied to future datasets without modifying code.

The HCAP subsample is extracted by filtering to inHCAP == 1 (N = 3,496).

Processing Steps

1. Threshold Classification (algorithm_thresholds)

Two intermediate threshold variables are computed before the final diagnosis is assigned.

cog_threshold — T-score Cognitive Performance Category

Condition cog_threshold Interpretation
TF < 37 2 Substantial impairment
TF < 48 (and ≥ 37) 1 Mild impairment
TF ≥ 48 0 Normal range

jorm_threshold — Informant-Rated Cognitive Change Category

Condition jorm_threshold Interpretation
jorm ≥ 3.4 2 Substantial worsening
3.0 < jorm < 3.4 1 Mild worsening
jorm ≤ 3.0 0 Stable or improved

The JORM scale runs from 1 (much improved) to 5 (much worse); a score of 3.0 represents “not much change.”

Self-report memory change

The PD102 values 8 (refused) and 9 (don’t know) are treated equivalently to 3 (worse) in the algorithm — ambiguous self-report responses are classified conservatively toward higher impairment.

The following code shows a function that uses these thresholds to create the data file.

algorithm_thresholds
function (df) 
{
    df <- df %>% mutate(cog_threshold = case_when(TF < 37 ~ 2, 
        TF < 48 ~ 1, !is.na(TF) ~ 0), jorm_threshold = case_when(jorm >= 
        3.4 ~ 2, jorm > 3 & jorm < 3.4 ~ 1, jorm <= 3 ~ 0))
    df
}
<bytecode: 0xbadbe7428>

2. V1 Classification Algorithm (v1_algorithm)

The final three-category diagnosis (dx_v1) is assigned using the following decision rules, applied in priority order. A visual of the algorithm is shown in Figure 5.

Primary Path — TF is Available

cog_threshold PD102 dx_v1 Label
2 (substantial) 3, 8, or 9 (worse/ambiguous) 3 Dementia
2 (substantial) 1 or 2 (same or better) 2 MCI
1 (mild) 3, 8, or 9 (worse/ambiguous) 2 MCI
1 (mild) 1 or 2 (same or better) 1 Normal
0 (normal range) Any 1 Normal

The logic requires both a substantially low cognitive score and self-reported worsening to reach a dementia classification. A low score without self-reported worsening, or self-reported worsening with only mild cognitive impairment, results in MCI.

Fallback Path — TF is Missing

When TF is unavailable (e.g., proxy interviews or missing cognitive data), the JORM informant rating is used alone:

jorm_threshold dx_v1 Label
2 3 Dementia
1 2 MCI
0 1 Normal

This is the code that creates a function that implements the algorithm shown in Figure 5.

v1_algorithm
function (df) 
{
    df <- df %>% mutate(dx_v1 = case_when(cog_threshold == 2 & 
        D102 %in% c(-8, 3, 8, 9) ~ 3, cog_threshold == 2 & D102 %in% 
        c(1, 2) ~ 2, cog_threshold == 1 & D102 %in% c(-8, 3, 
        8, 9) ~ 2, cog_threshold == 1 & D102 %in% c(1, 2) ~ 1, 
        cog_threshold == 0 ~ 1, is.na(TF) & jorm_threshold == 
            2 ~ 3, is.na(TF) & jorm_threshold == 1 ~ 2, is.na(TF) & 
            jorm_threshold == 0 ~ 1))
    df <- df %>% labelled::set_variable_labels(dx_v1 = "Algorithm (V1) Dx") %>% 
        labelled::set_value_labels(dx_v1 = c(Normal = 1, MCI = 2, 
            Dementia = 3))
    df
}
<bytecode: 0xbad4a6bd8>
